ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The experiment was overseen by the first author's university human subjects' ethics review board.
The study was approved by the first author's university human subjects' ethics review board.
We recruited seventy-nine native speakers of Tagalog for the experiment via Prolific.co (mean age =36.58; Range = 18-59).
All participants gave their informed consent and were remunerated £3.13 for the 30-minute experiment.

Participants were instructed to find a quiet area and sit in front of their computer wearing Before the experiment, participants were first given 6 practice trials to familiarize them with the slightly strange stimuli and task.
After the two experimental blocks, participants were asked to fill out a language questionnaire, and this completed the procedure.
Four participants were further removed as they reported another Philippine language as their native language (5.79%) in the language questionnaire.
Sixty-five participants were retained for further analyses.
All participants provided informed consent prior to participation.

Participants were instructed to respond as quickly and as accurately as possible to each target, with a time-out of 2000 ms; participants who failed to respond within 2000 ms of trial offset received a visual time-out message ('no response detected') and were then presented with the subsequent trial.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. #### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 402 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (402). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 79 columns across 5 data files.
#### Issues Identified

4 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("Auditory_Resid-Trimmed-CorrectAnswers-April29.csv", "Auditory_Voiced-Voiceless-April29.csv", "Supplementary Material A.xlsx", "Supplementary Material A.xlsx"), Column = c("Participant.Browser", "Participant.Browser", "RelPrime(Freq)", "Target (PerMF)"), Issues = c("🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Values look like personal information: ip_address (11500 values, 100%)", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Values look like personal information: ip_address (2329 values, 100%)", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 99% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"CVC", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 100% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"PrimeLength\"" )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 5 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: We recruited seventy-nine native speakers of Tagalog for the experiment via Prolific.co (mean age =36.58; Range = 18-59).
All participants gave their informed consent and were remunerated £3.13 for the 30-minute experiment.

Participants were instructed to find a quiet area and sit in front of their computer wearing Before the experiment, participants were first given 6 practice trials to familiarize them with the slightly strange stimuli and task.
After the two experimental blocks, participants were asked to fill out a language questionnaire, and this completed the procedure.
Four participants were further removed as they reported another Philippine language as their native language (5.79%) in the language questionnaire.
Sixty-five participants were retained for further analyses.
All participants provided informed consent prior to participation.

Participants were instructed to respond as quickly and as accurately as possible to each target, with a time-out of 2000 ms; participants who failed to respond within 2000 ms of trial offset received a visual time-out message ('no response detected') and were then presented with the subsequent trial.

text.text: To comprehend speech, the auditory system segments a continuous input stream at various levels (e.g., sounds, words).

Previous studies have shown that listeners also segment complex spoken words like treatment into their morphological units /ˈtriːt/+/mənt/, where there is a clear morphological boundary between /stem/+/affix/.
Here, we report an auditory masked priming experiment in Tagalog investigating whether complex spoken words with obscured morphological identity and boundaries are segmented into morphemes.

We compare the processing of prefixed words [1] without morphophonological alternations (NOCHANGE, e.g., /maŋ/+/híla/ becomes maŋhíla 'to pull'), [2] with nasal ASSIMILATION obscuring prefix identity (e.g., /maŋ/+/búlag/ becomes mambúlag 'to blind'), and [3] with nasal SUBSTITUTION obscuring both prefix and stem identities and their phonological boundary (e.g., /maŋ/+/túlak/ becomes manúlak 'to push').
Crucially, these morphophonological alternations exhibit variability: nasal SUBSTITUTION is more likely for VOICELESS-initial stems than for VOICEDinitial stems.
We found significant priming effects of similar magnitude across NOCHANGE, ASSIMILATION, and SUBSTITUTION conditions.
These effects are morphological in nature since no reliable priming was observed for monomorphemic word pairs with phonological overlap.
Further, similar priming was found for both VOICELESS and VOICED SUBSTITUTION conditions.

These findings unambiguously show that spoken prefixed words are decomposed into morphemes, thereby supporting auditory processing models and morphological theories which argue that morphologically complex words are stored and accessed as morphemes in the mental lexicon.

Ultimately, we provide clear evidence that automatic decomposition in speech comprehension is robust in the face of variable morphophonological alternations that obscure prefix identity and morphological boundaries.
A central question in the study of the mental lexicon is how morphological structure plays a role in (pre)lexical processing.

In spoken word recognition, competing models differ in how morphologically complex words are represented and accessed in the mental lexicon, ranging from holistic accounts-in which such words are stored as whole words (e.g., Tyler, 1988)to decompositional accounts that posit morphological parsing during recognition (e.g., Marslen-Wilson et al., 1994).
text.formatted: In spoken word recognition, competing models differ in how morphologically complex words are represented and accessed in the mental lexicon, ranging from holistic accounts-in which such words are stored as whole words (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Tyler, 1988</ref>)to decompositional accounts that posit morphological parsing during recognition (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Marslen-Wilson et al., 1994)</ref>.

text.text: A large body of psycholinguistic evidence supports the latter, suggesting that morphologically complex words are represented and accessed as constituent morphemes during speech comprehension.
However, the mechanisms of decomposition during spoken word recognition remain less well understood than in visual word recognition, where visual linguistic information is provided all at once.
Whether comparable early decomposition operates during speech comprehension, where auditory information unfolds over time, is less clear.

Moreover, most of the morphological types previously investigated in both auditory and visual domains involve cases where there is a transparent morphological boundary between the affix and the stem (e.g., treatment as /ˈtriːt /+/mənt/, thinking as /ˈθɪŋk/+/ɪŋ/), which makes decomposition more straightforward.
Whether auditory decomposition also occurs when morphological identity and boundaries are obscured by morphophonological alternations is less well investigated.

In the present study, we address these issues by examining the role of morphological information during speech comprehension, particularly examining Tagalog prefixed words with phonologically obscured prefix identity and phonologically obscured /prefix/+/stem/ boundaries.
One of the most widely used paradigms for investigating morphological decomposition is visual masked priming (Forster, 1988).
text.formatted: One of the most widely used paradigms for investigating morphological decomposition is visual masked priming <ref type="bibr">(Forster, 1988)</ref>.

text.text: In this paradigm, a morphologically simple target (e.g., CLEAN) is preceded by a briefly presented prime (typically <60 ms), such as a morphologically related word (e.g., cleaner) or an unrelated control (e.g., people), presented too quickly for conscious awareness.
text.formatted: In this paradigm, a morphologically simple target (e.g., CLEAN) is preceded by a briefly presented prime (typically <60 ms), such as a morphologically related word (e.g., cleaner) or an unrelated control (e.g., people), presented too quickly for conscious awareness.

text.text: The prime is usually preceded by a forward mask (e.g., ########) and, in some cases, followed by a backward mask.

Critically, the paradigm includes control conditions to isolate morphological effects: an orthographic control, consisting of monomorphemic pairs with form overlap (e.g., scandal-SCAN), and a semantic control, consisting of semantically related pairs (e.g., dog-CAT).
Robust priming effects are observed for morphologically related pairs, but not for orthographic or semantic controls (see Rastle & Davis, 2008; Cayado & Rastle, 2025 for reviews).
text.formatted: Robust priming effects are observed for morphologically related pairs, but not for orthographic or semantic controls (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Rastle & Davis, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cayado & Rastle, 2025</ref> for reviews).

text.text: Moreover, priming is also found for pseudo-morphological pairs (e.g., brother-BROTH) (Rastle et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Moreover, priming is also found for pseudo-morphological pairs (e.g., brother-BROTH) <ref type="bibr">(Rastle et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: This pattern of findings suggests that morphological decomposition in the visual domain operates rapidly and early in lexical processing, prior to the availability of grammatical and semantic information (Rastle et al., 2000; Rastle et al., 2004).
text.formatted: This pattern of findings suggests that morphological decomposition in the visual domain operates rapidly and early in lexical processing, prior to the availability of grammatical and semantic information <ref type="bibr">(Rastle et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Rastle et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: It has been shown that input modality has an effect on the decomposition of complex words.

Specifically, Beyersmann et al. (2020) showed that parsing suffixed words into morphological pieces appears to be easier in the visual domain than in the auditory domain, which is likely to reflect the way linguistic information is presented in the two domains.
text.formatted: Specifically, <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Beyersmann et al. (2020)</ref> showed that parsing suffixed words into morphological pieces appears to be easier in the visual domain than in the auditory domain, which is likely to reflect the way linguistic information is presented in the two domains.

text.text: Orthographic information is provided all at once in visual word recognition, which lessens the effects of competition with other words with similar orthographic onsets during processing.

In contrast, auditory linguistic information unfolds over time, forcing the listener to select between co-activated word and morphological competitors with similar phonological onsets (Marslen-Wilson, 1987; Balling & Baayen, 2012).
text.formatted: In contrast, auditory linguistic information unfolds over time, forcing the listener to select between co-activated word and morphological competitors with similar phonological onsets <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Marslen-Wilson, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Balling & Baayen, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Further, in languages like English, print-tomeaning mapping of morphemes is typically more consistent than sound-to-meaning mapping, which could emphasise the presence of morphological structure in the visual domain (Rastle, 2019), possibly making decomposition more straightforward in visual word recognition.
text.formatted: Further, in languages like English, print-tomeaning mapping of morphemes is typically more consistent than sound-to-meaning mapping, which could emphasise the presence of morphological structure in the visual domain <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Rastle, 2019)</ref>, possibly making decomposition more straightforward in visual word recognition.

text.text: This warrants further auditory experiments to uncover how decomposition could vary in visual and auditory modalities, and across a wider range of languages.

Although less investigated compared to visual word recognition, whether and how morphological information plays a role during speech comprehension has been investigated using different paradigms, such as cross-modal priming (Marslen-Wilson et al., 1994; Gonnerman et al., 2007; Smolka et al., 2018; Wynne et al., 2021), auditory priming (Creemers & Embick, 2021; Creemers et al., 2020 Creemers et al., , 2023;; Wilder et al., 2019; Bacovcin et al., 2017), auditory masked priming (Kouider & Dupoux, 2005; Ussishkin et al., 2015 Ussishkin et al., , 2017 Ussishkin et al., , 2025;; Geary & Ussishkin, 2019), and single word auditory lexical decision tasks with electroencephalography (EEG, Beyersmann et al., 2019) and magnetoencephalography (MEG, Matar & Marantz, 2025; Gwilliams & Marantz, 2015).
text.formatted: Although less investigated compared to visual word recognition, whether and how morphological information plays a role during speech comprehension has been investigated using different paradigms, such as cross-modal priming <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Marslen-Wilson et al., 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Gonnerman et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Smolka et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Wynne et al., 2021)</ref>, auditory priming <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Creemers & Embick, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Creemers et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Creemers et al., , 2023;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Wilder et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bacovcin et al., 2017)</ref>, auditory masked priming <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Kouider & Dupoux, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Ussishkin et al., 2015</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Ussishkin et al., , 2017</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Ussishkin et al., , 2025;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Geary & Ussishkin, 2019)</ref>, and single word auditory lexical decision tasks with electroencephalography <ref type="bibr">(EEG, Beyersmann et al., 2019)</ref> and magnetoencephalography (MEG, <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Matar & Marantz, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Gwilliams & Marantz, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Across these paradigms, the evidence generated suggests that morphologically complex words are decomposed into morphemes in speech comprehension.

These findings are consistent with spoken word recognition models that require decomposition (e.g., Marslen-Wilson et al., 1994; Balling & Baayen, 2012), as well as morphological theories arguing that morphologically complex words are represented and accessed in terms of morphemes (Halle & Marantz, 1993; Embick, 2015).
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with spoken word recognition models that require decomposition (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Marslen-Wilson et al., 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Balling & Baayen, 2012)</ref>, as well as morphological theories arguing that morphologically complex words are represented and accessed in terms of morphemes <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Halle & Marantz, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Embick, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Using auditory priming with a lexical decision task, Creemers et al. (2023) found that English speakers recognize target words like treat, pig, and cash more quickly when they are auditorily preceded by prime words like treatment (real suffixed), pigment (pseudosuffixed), and cashew (nonsuffixed), respectively, although significantly larger priming was observed for the real suffixed condition. Wilder et al. (2019) also found that English speakers responded significantly faster to complex targets like frogs when they are auditorily preceded by their stems (e.g., frog).
text.formatted: Using auditory priming with a lexical decision task, <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Creemers et al. (2023)</ref> found that English speakers recognize target words like treat, pig, and cash more quickly when they are auditorily preceded by prime words like treatment (real suffixed), pigment (pseudosuffixed), and cashew (nonsuffixed), respectively, although significantly larger priming was observed for the real suffixed condition. <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Wilder et al. (2019)</ref> also found that English speakers responded significantly faster to complex targets like frogs when they are auditorily preceded by their stems (e.g., frog).

text.text: In a rhyme priming task, priming effects have also been observed when morphologically complex targets like snowed are preceded by a prime that rhymes with the target's stem (e.g., dough rhymes with snow, Bacovcin et al., 2017).
text.formatted: In a rhyme priming task, priming effects have also been observed when morphologically complex targets like snowed are preceded by a prime that rhymes with the target's stem (e.g., dough rhymes with snow, <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bacovcin et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In other Indo-European languages like Dutch and German, priming effects have also been obtained for prefixed words, where responses to target words like halen 'take/get' were facilitated by semantically transparent primes (e.g., afhalen 'take away/out') and semantically opaque primes (e.g., herhalen 'repeat', Creemers et al., 2020; Creemers & Embick, 2021; Smolka et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In other Indo-European languages like Dutch and German, priming effects have also been obtained for prefixed words, where responses to target words like halen 'take/get' were facilitated by semantically transparent primes (e.g., afhalen 'take away/out') and semantically opaque primes (e.g., herhalen 'repeat', <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Creemers et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Creemers & Embick, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Smolka et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Findings from these studies provide evidence that speech comprehension also involves a decomposition stage.

However, the auditory studies discussed above employed unmasked priming paradigms, making their findings difficult to compare directly with visual masked priming evidence that argues decomposition is rapid and occurs prior to semantic access.
The first successful demonstration of auditory masked priming was provided by Kouider and Dupoux (2005) in French.
text.formatted: The first successful demonstration of auditory masked priming was provided by <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Kouider and Dupoux (2005)</ref> in French.

text.text: In their study, auditory primes were durationally compressed at varying rates (35%, 40%, 50%, 70%) and embedded in a stream of spectrally similar, unintelligible sound made of reversed recordings of speech.
Prime-target pairs were related morphologically, phonologically, semantically, or by identity, with morphological pairs consisting of masculine primes and feminine targets (e.g., cousin-cousine).
Participants remained unaware of primes at 35% and 40% compression rates, but reported awareness at 50% and 70%.
At the strongest compression rate (35%), robust priming was observed only in the identity condition, with no effects for morphological, phonological, or semantic relationships.
Morphological priming emerged only at 50% and 70% compression rates, when primes were no longer fully masked.
No phonological priming was observed at any compression rate, while semantic priming was found only at 70%.
Overall, this pattern of results shows that lexical processing occurs at an early and unconscious stage of speech processing before access to meaning.
Using the same auditory masked priming technique, Ussishkin et al. (2015) investigated the effects of nonconcatenative morphology in Maltese word recognition.
text.formatted: Using the same auditory masked priming technique, <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Ussishkin et al. (2015)</ref> investigated the effects of nonconcatenative morphology in Maltese word recognition.

text.text: In contrast to Kouider and Dupoux (2005), they reported robust priming effects for identical word pairs (e.g., giddem-giddem 'to gnaw') and for pairs sharing a triconsonantal root (e.g., ngidem-giddem 'to be bitten-to gnaw', both derived from √gdm) at a 35% compression rate.
text.formatted: In contrast to <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Kouider and Dupoux (2005)</ref>, they reported robust priming effects for identical word pairs (e.g., giddem-giddem 'to gnaw') and for pairs sharing a triconsonantal root (e.g., ngidem-giddem 'to be bitten-to gnaw', both derived from √gdm) at a 35% compression rate.

text.text: Crucially, no priming was observed for phonologically similar pairs, indicating that the effect was morphological rather than purely phonological.

However, no reliable priming emerged for pairs sharing only a word pattern (e.g., kiber-siket 'to grow-to be quiet', both instantiating the C1VC2VC3 verbal template; see also Ussishkin et al., 2025 for converging evidence).
text.formatted: However, no reliable priming emerged for pairs sharing only a word pattern (e.g., kiber-siket 'to grow-to be quiet', both instantiating the C1VC2VC3 verbal template; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Ussishkin et al., 2025</ref> for converging evidence).

text.text: A subsequent reanalysis using computational modelling further showed that semantic information contributes to lexical access during spoken word recognition, as reflected in significant effects of semantic measures on reaction times (Nieder et al., 2024).
text.formatted: A subsequent reanalysis using computational modelling further showed that semantic information contributes to lexical access during spoken word recognition, as reflected in significant effects of semantic measures on reaction times <ref type="bibr">(Nieder et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, these semantic effects were observed at target offset but not at target onset, consistent with models that posit semantic contributions arise relatively late in the processing stream after morphological decomposition.
Further evidence that early decomposition in speech comprehension occurs prior to semantic access comes from research on other Semitic languages.

In Hebrew, Geary and Ussishkin (2019) reported significant masked auditory priming effects for word pairs sharing a root morpheme both with a transparent semantic relationship (e.g., poreʦ~priʦa 'burglarburglary') and without a transparent semantic relationship (e.g., mifraʦ~priʦa 'gulfburglary').
text.formatted: In Hebrew, <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Geary and Ussishkin (2019)</ref> reported significant masked auditory priming effects for word pairs sharing a root morpheme both with a transparent semantic relationship (e.g., poreʦ~priʦa 'burglarburglary') and without a transparent semantic relationship (e.g., mifraʦ~priʦa 'gulfburglary').

text.text: These findings suggest that early decomposition operates independently of meaning during speech comprehension.

Taken together, results from Maltese and Hebrew provide support for models of speech comprehension that posit an early decomposition stage (e.g., Taft et al., 1986; Marslen-Wilson et al., 1994; Balling & Baayen, 2012).
text.formatted: Taken together, results from Maltese and Hebrew provide support for models of speech comprehension that posit an early decomposition stage (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Taft et al., 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Marslen-Wilson et al., 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Balling & Baayen, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: However, evidence from French and Maltese word patterns shows no reliable morphological priming at the shortest prime compression rates, indicating that auditory masked morphological priming effects may be language-or morphology-dependent.
It is therefore crucial to test whether auditory masked priming consistently supports models of early, automatic decomposition across a wider range of languages and morphological systems.

Whether listeners recognise roots with obscured surface realisation due to phonological alternations is another issue in spoken word recognition. Marslen-Wilson and Zhou (1999) addressed this question using a delayed auditory-auditory priming paradigm with English vowel change.
text.formatted: Whether listeners recognise roots with obscured surface realisation due to phonological alternations is another issue in spoken word recognition. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Marslen-Wilson and Zhou (1999)</ref> addressed this question using a delayed auditory-auditory priming paradigm with English vowel change.

text.text: They found that suffixed words like sanity significantly facilitated access to the stem sane and other suffixed words like sanely, even though the phonological realization of the vowels in sane and sanity are distinct.
Similar activation also occurs even when the initial segment of the root is obscured.

For instance, in an auditory masked priming experiment, Ussishkin et al. (2017) examined Scottish Gaelic, where consonant mutation obscures the initial segment of the root (e.g., pòg 'kiss' begins with [p h ], but phòg 'kissed' begins with [f]).
text.formatted: For instance, in an auditory masked priming experiment, <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Ussishkin et al. (2017)</ref> examined Scottish Gaelic, where consonant mutation obscures the initial segment of the root (e.g., pòg 'kiss' begins with [p h ], but phòg 'kissed' begins with [f]).

text.text: They found reliable priming effects for the identity condition and the morphological condition at a 35% prime compression rate, where the prime is the mutated past tense form of the target, while no such effects were obtained for the phonological control and semantic control conditions.
Findings from these studies suggest that listeners are able to recognize roots regardless of vowel changes and consonant mutation that obscure the phonological identity of the roots.
However, Pizarro-Guevara (2017) identified a case where morphological processing does seem to be affected by morphophonological alternations.
Using auditory masked priming, Pizarro-Guevara (2017) investigated whether nasal substitution in Dabaw Bisaya (Austronesian, Philippines) hampers decomposition of spoken prefixed words.

In Dabaw Bisaya, adding a velar-final prefix, naŋ-, which encodes pluractionality, to an obstruent-initial stem triggers nasal substitution, where the prefix-final nasal and the root-initial obstruent coalesce into one sound (e.g., /naŋ-/+/patid/ 'kick' becomes namatid 'kicked (multiple people or things)'), thereby obscuring the phonological identity of the prefix and the stem, as well as the morphological boundary.
Significant priming effects emerged for prefixed words with no morphophonological alternation, while no such effects were found for those that underwent nasal substitution.
These findings suggest that decomposition in auditory lexical processing can break down in the face of morphophonological alternations that obscure morphological identity and boundaries.

These contrasting findings warrant further investigation of what kind of morphophonological alternations hamper decomposition in spoken word recognition.

Although the cases of consonant mutation in Scottish Gaelic and vowel change in English show that decomposition remains operational in the face of some morphophonological alternations in the stem, the morphological boundary is still transparent in these cases.
The case of Dabaw Bisaya opens the possibility that obscuring the boundary between two overt morphemes (i.e., prefix and stem) prevents decomposition.

However, it is also possible that Pizarro-Guevara's study is underpowered, since they only included 15 experimental items in their substitution condition, resulting in 960 data points with 64 participants, far from the recommended 1600 data points (see Brysbaert & Stevens, 2018).

text.text: The present study, therefore, revisits the question of whether obscuring the morphological boundary between two overt morphemes hampers auditory decomposition.
Exploring this question is of prime importance as it will shed light on what factors trigger decomposition in spoken word recognition.
In the present study, we address this problem using Tagalog, particularly looking at nasal assimilation and nasal substitution, which will be discussed in turn.
In Tagalog (Austronesian, Philippines), affixing velar-final prefixes like /maŋ-, paŋ-, naŋ-/ to obstruent-initial stems can trigger one of two morphophonological alternations.
First, the prefix-final velar nasal can take on the place of articulation of the initial sound of the stem, resulting in NASAL ASSIMILATION.
For example, the velar nasal in maŋ-becomes mam-in mambúlag 'to blind (someone)'.
NASAL ASSIMILATION is also triggered by liquid sonorants, surfacing as pan-/man-/nan-for l-and ɾ-initial stems.

The phonological identity of the stem remains unchanged in NASAL ASSIMILATION, since there is no coalescence between the final velar sound in the prefix and the initial consonant in the stem (see Table 2A for examples).
text.formatted: The phonological identity of the stem remains unchanged in NASAL ASSIMILATION, since there is no coalescence between the final velar sound in the prefix and the initial consonant in the stem (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">2A</ref> for examples).

text.text: Alternatively, the prefix-final velar nasal and the initial obstruent of the stem can coalesce resulting in a single nasal stop with the same place of articulation as the stem's original obstruent, resulting in NASAL SUBSTITUTION (Schacter & Otanes, 1972; Zuraw, 2010), like in Dabaw Bisaya.
text.formatted: Alternatively, the prefix-final velar nasal and the initial obstruent of the stem can coalesce resulting in a single nasal stop with the same place of articulation as the stem's original obstruent, resulting in NASAL SUBSTITUTION <ref type="bibr">(Schacter & Otanes, 1972;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Zuraw, 2010)</ref>, like in Dabaw Bisaya.

text.text: For example, the velar nasal in maŋ-and the initial consonant in túlak 'push' become one sound n in manúlak 'to push someone'.

The phonological form of the prefix and the stem both change, and the morphological boundary between them is obscured at orthographic and phonological levels due to the coalescence of the prefix-final and the steminitial segments (See Table 2B for more examples).

text.text: The Dabaw Bisaya results suggest that NASAL SUBSTITUTION poses a problem for decomposition into morphemes during spoken word recognition.

These prefixes have various derivational and inflectional purposes: maŋ-marks agent voice, naŋ-marks perfective aspect, and paŋ-typically creates reservational (e.g., /paŋ/+/ paléŋke/ 'market' becomes [pamaléŋke] 'for wearing at the market') and instrumental (e.g., /paŋ/+/púnas/ 'wipe' becomes [pamúnas] 'for use in wiping') adjectives (Schachter & Otanes, 1972). illustrate, when Tagalog listeners hear the phonological input mam, they could parse this as the maŋ-prefix after nasal assimilation (e.g., mam-búlag 'to blind' from /maŋ/+/ búlag/) or as the maŋ-prefix after nasal substitution (e.g., ma-mangká 'to ride a boat' from /maŋ/+/ baŋká/, which begins with the phonological sequence ma-) or even as the ma-prefixfoot_0 and the beginning of an m-initial stem (ma-múlat 'to open eyes').

text.text: This indeterminacy may lead the parser to either delay morphological decomposition, or to make errors.

For example, mamangká and mamúlat could be erroneously parsed into /mam/+/angká/* and /mam/+/úlat/*, respectively, which are phonotactically illegal, since vowel-initial stems do not exist in Tagalog.

However, the phonological sequence maN is followed by a consonant (/p, t, k, ʔ, b, d, g, m, n, ŋ, s, h, l, r, w, j/) in the case of nasal assimilation, while it is followed by a vowel (/a, e, i, o, u/) in the case of nasal substitution and when ma-is prefixed to a nasal initial stem.
Perhaps, Tagalog listeners can exploit these phonological sequences as cues (i.e., maN+consonant or maN+vowel) to avoid misparsing during auditory word recognition.
Previous work has investigated whether nasal assimilation and nasal substitution hamper decomposition in visual word recognition.

Specifically, Cayado et al. (2025) report behavioural masked priming and MEG evidence that skilled Tagalog readers decompose prefixed words that undergo nasal substitution and assimilation just as they decompose complex words with no alternation.
However, Cayado et al.'s findings only address obscurity at the orthographic level (e.g., mang + bangka 'boat' = mamangka 'to ride a boat'), since they focused on visual word recognition.

It, therefore, remains an empirical question whether variable morphophonological alternations negatively impact decomposition in spoken word recognition, where co-activated nasal-assimilated and nasal-substituted words may compete with each other and listeners are likely to make misparsings as the auditory information is processed incrementally.

Using an auditory masked priming paradigm, the present study investigates [1] if obscured morphological identity in the prefix hampers auditory decomposition; [2] if obscured morphological boundaries hamper auditory decomposition; and [3] if variability in phonological patterns modulates auditory decomposition.

If decomposition is hampered by obscured morphological identity in the prefix, then reliable priming should only be obtained for prefixed words with no morphophonological alternation, while no such effects should be obtained for prefixed words with NASAL ASSIMILATION and NASAL SUBSTITUTION.
In contrast, if decomposition remains operational despite obscured morphological identity, then reliable priming should be obtained for all 3 types of prefixed words.

If an obscured morphological boundary between the /prefix/+/stem/ hampers decomposition, then reliable priming should only be obtained for prefixed words with either no morphophonological alternation or with NASAL ASSIMILATION, but not for prefixed words with NASAL SUBSTITUTION.
However, if auditory decomposition is unaffected by obscured morphological boundaries, then reliable priming should be obtained for all 3 types of prefixed words.

Finally, if variability in phonological patterns modulates decomposition, then larger priming effects should be obtained for nasal-substituted prefixed words with VOICELESS-INITIAL stems than VOICED-INITIAL stems, since nasal substitution is more likely to occur for voiceless-initial stems than voiced-initial stems.
Similar priming should be obtained if phonological variability does not modulate decomposition in speech comprehension.
We recruited seventy-nine native speakers of Tagalog for the experiment via Prolific.co (mean age =36.58; Range = 18-59).
Participants reported their city of origin in the Philippines.
Only participants from cities where Tagalog is the dominant language were retained.
Due to the multilingual nature of the Philippines, all participants also reported speaking English.
Others additionally spoke another Philippine language (N=39), Spanish (N=4), Japanese (N=3), French (N=2), Mandarin Chinese (N=1), Thai (N=1), German (N=1), Italian (N=1), and Korean (N=1).
All participants reported completing their primary and secondary education in the Philippines.
The experiment was overseen by the first author's university human subjects' ethics review board.
All participants gave their informed consent and were remunerated £3.13 for the 30-minute experiment.

text.text: We included the IDENTITY condition to test the viability of auditory masked priming in Tagalog and in a fully online setting (all previous auditory masked priming experiments were conducted in a lab setting).

Further, the PHONOLOGICAL condition was included to establish that the priming obtained in the critical conditions is not just due to the sounds they share but their morphological relationship. 6 practice trials were also added, consisting of 3 real words and 3 nonwords that were not used in the test phase.

text.text: The experiment included 200 nonword targets and 100 nonword primes as filler items.
All nonwords were pronounceable and ranged from 5 to 10 letters in length to align with the critical and control items.
To prevent participants from anticipating the lexical decision task, half of the nonword targets (100) were paired with real word primes that were 6 to 10 letters long.
Both nonword and real word primes were matched by length across lists.
In total, the experiment consisted of 406 trials.
All items, once selected, were subsequently recorded by a male native speaker of Tagalog.
All items were recorded in a sound-attenuated Whisper Room booth at a sampling rate of 44,110 Hz.
The native speaker read each item from a list in a relaxed yet careful manner.
Recordings were made while the speaker wore an omnidirectional head-mounted SM10A microphone made by Shure, which was connected via a Symetrix Audio 302 pre-amplifier to an Alesis Masterlink 9600.
The speaker pronounced each item three times, and the best token of the three was selected for use in our experiment.
'Best token' was generally defined as the token with the clearest production, the most neutral intonation (i.e., standard declarative), and no non-linguistic intrusions (e.g., coughs).
We demarcated, labelled, and extracted this token in Praat (Boersma & Weenink, 2011).

text.text: First, the prime-target pairs were matched with an auditory mask consisting of five unrelated Tagalog words with a very low phonological overlap with the prime and target.
The words utilized as masks were recorded as part of the recording session described above.

Second, all stimuli in the experiment-targets, primes, and masks-were scaled to match the global average RMS level across all recordings (approximately 82dB SPL) before being concatenated into stimuli.
Third, primes and masks were durationally compressed to 35% of their original duration using the P(itch) S(ynchronous) O(ver)L(ap) A(dd) (PSOLA) algorithm, and their intensity downscaled to 15dB.
This compression rate ensures that the prime is subliminally presented (see Kouider & Dupoux, 2005).

text.text: Fourth, masks were temporally reversed.

Finally, the components were concatenated into a single speech stream, such that a target (played at a normal speech rate and unattenuated) was superimposed on this stream, with its onset coinciding with the prime's offset, followed by four consecutive masks.

They were told that "imagine you are at a party.

Listen for that thing and decide whether it is a word you know or not."
The experimental items were then presented in two blocks, with 200 trials each.
All participants heard the targets in both related and unrelated prime contexts.
Targets were only heard once per block, and the blocks were interrupted by a short break to minimize long-lag priming effects.

After the two experimental blocks, participants were asked to fill out a language questionnaire, and this completed the procedure.

The main goals of the present study were three-fold: first, we tested whether obscuring the morphological identity of the prefix hampers decomposition; second, we examined whether obscuring the morphological boundary of a /prefix/+/stem/ hampers decomposition; and third, The majority of morphological processing studies have focused on written words, where all orthographic information is available simultaneously.
Whether comparable decomposition processes operate during speech comprehension remains less well understood.

The present findings extend this literature across several dimensions: modality, by focusing on speech comprehension; typological breadth, by examining an understudied language such as Tagalog; ontological scope, by investigating underexplored morphophonological patterns; and methodology, by demonstrating that masked auditory priming can be conducted in a fully online setting.
This methodological advance opens new possibilities for research by enabling access to more diverse participant populations and reducing the resource demands associated with lab-based experiments.

Crucially, with respect to morphology, the priming effects observed here are consistent with the prediction that nasal-assimilated and nasal-substituted prefixed forms facilitate lexical access to their corresponding unchanged stems.

This facilitation cannot be attributed to phonological overlap, as no priming was found for monomorphemic word pairs sharing the same second syllable, or semantic relatedness, given that masked priming effects have not been observed when masked at this compression rate.

Further, these priming effects emerged early during speech comprehension, since the primes were compressed to 35% of their original duration and only available for ~0.260 seconds (prime durations prior to compression averaged 0.745 seconds).

The auditory masked priming effects observed in this study are consistent with what has been found in consonantal roots in Maltese (Ussishkin et al., 2015 (Ussishkin et al., , 2025) ) and Hebrew (e.g., Geary & Ussishkin, 2019), as well as initial consonant mutation in Scottish Gaelic (Ussishkin et al., 2017), but inconsistent with the lack of priming in word patterns in Maltese (Ussishkin et al., 2015 (Ussishkin et al., , 2025) ) and nasalsubstituted prefixed words in Dabaw Bisaya (Pizarro-Guevara, 2017).

text.text: How, then, do listeners process and store words with morphophonological alternations?
In English, it has been observed that listeners can link stems with vowel change (e.g., sanity) to their unchanged forms (e.g., sane, sanely) in the mental lexicon (Marslen-Wilson & Zhou, 1999).
text.formatted: In English, it has been observed that listeners can link stems with vowel change (e.g., sanity) to their unchanged forms (e.g., sane, sanely) in the mental lexicon <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Marslen-Wilson & Zhou, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: In Scottish Gaelic, Ussishkin et al. (2017) revealed that native listeners were able to link the mutated (e.g., phòg 'kissed' with [f]) and unmutated forms (e.g., pòg 'kiss' with [p h ]) in the mental lexicon, and such linking happens early during processing as the primes were presented very quickly (i.e., compressed to 35% of their original duration), as in the current study.

(2017)</ref> revealed that native listeners were able to link the mutated (e.g., phòg 'kissed' with [f]) and unmutated forms (e.g., pòg 'kiss' with [p h ]) in the mental lexicon, and such linking happens early during processing as the primes were presented very quickly (i.e., compressed to 35% of their original duration), as in the current study.

text.text: These studies provide evidence that decomposition remains robust in the face of morphophonological alternations, consistent with what has been found in the present study.

However, the case of Tagalog is different: first, unlike Scottish Gaelic, nasal assimilation and nasal substitution are triggered by a linear prefixation process, where there are at least two overt morphemes; second, nasal assimilation and nasal substitution exhibit variability-it is not completely predictable whether nasal assimilation or nasal substitution will take place when velar-final prefixes are attached to obstruent-initial stems.

Therefore, results from our experiment shed light as to how native Tagalog listeners retrieve morphological pieces, especially when the prefix is phonologically obscured in the case of nasal assimilation and when both prefix and stem as well as their morphological boundary are phonologically obscured due to nasal substitution.

We showed that hearing masked and compressed primes like mambúlag 'to blind (someone)' (from /maŋ-/+/búlag/) results in faster lexical decision to non-compressed targets like búlag, despite the nasalassimilated prefix form.
Further, hearing masked and compressed nasal-substituted primes like mamitás 'to pick a flower' (from/maŋ-/+/pitás/) also resulted in faster lexical decision to noncompressed targets like pitás.

Our results indicate that Tagalog listeners successfully decomposed masked and compressed primes into constituent morphemes, despite the fact that nasal assimilation obscures the phonological identity of the prefix and nasal substitution obscures the phonological identity of both the prefix and the stem, as well as their morphological boundary.

In the case of nasal substitution, Tagalog listeners appear to be capable of linking the obscured form of the stem (e.g., mitas from mamitás) to its default form (e.g., pitás) at a very early stage of speech comprehension, consistent with what has been observed in Scottish Gaelic (Ussishkin et al., 2017).
text.formatted: In the case of nasal substitution, Tagalog listeners appear to be capable of linking the obscured form of the stem (e.g., mitas from mamitás) to its default form (e.g., pitás) at a very early stage of speech comprehension, consistent with what has been observed in Scottish Gaelic <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Ussishkin et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: It is possible that listeners exploit the place of articulation in the surface coalesced nasal (i.e., m in mamitás) as a cue to recover the underlying obstruent of the stem (i.e., p in pitás).

Finally, the way Tagalog listeners link these obscured stem forms to their unchanged stem forms are at a similar level of ease as linking two unchanged stem forms, as in the case of words that do not undergo any morphophonological alternations (e.g., maŋhúla 'to guess' linking to húla).
Unlike the case of Scottish Gaelic where initial consonant mutations are categorical, nasal assimilation and nasal substitution in Tagalog exhibit phonologically patterned variability.

Specifically, when velar-final prefixes like /maŋ-/ are attached to obstruent-initial stems (e.g., p, t, s, k, b, d, g), it is not totally predictable whether assimilation or substitution will happen, but there are phonological trends-nasal substitution is more likely than nasal assimilation for voiceless-initial stems while the opposite holds for voiced-initial stems (Zuraw, 2010).
text.formatted: Specifically, when velar-final prefixes like /maŋ-/ are attached to obstruent-initial stems (e.g., p, t, s, k, b, d, g), it is not totally predictable whether assimilation or substitution will happen, but there are phonological trends-nasal substitution is more likely than nasal assimilation for voiceless-initial stems while the opposite holds for voiced-initial stems <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Zuraw, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: We initially predicted that that such variability may result in occasional misparsing, thereby adding another level of processing difficulty when detecting the morphological boundary between prefix and stem.

For example, when Tagalog listeners hear the input stream mam, the second nasal could belong to the prefix in assimilation (e.g., /maŋ-/+/búlag/ becomes mam-búlag 'to blind') or to the stem in substitution (e.g., /maŋ-/+/bangká/ becomes ma-mangka 'to go boating') or to the stem in ma-prefixed words attached to m-initial stems (e.g., ma-múlat 'to open eyes').
We hypothesized that the uncertainty that this induces may disrupt the retrieval of morphemes.

However, we found that decomposition in auditory word recognition remains robust and operational in the face morphophonological variability, as evidenced by the similar magnitude of priming effects for ASSIMILATION and SUBSTITUTION conditions, and for both the VOICED and VOICELESS SUBSTITUTION sub-conditions.
It seems that native Tagalog listeners do not experience any difficulties with parsing such items.
How, then, does decomposition happen during speech comprehension, particularly when the morphemes are obscured?
A proposal by Cayado et al. (2025) for visual word recognition can also apply to spoken word recognition.
Note that phonological sequences like maN, naN, and paN occur mostly in the context of prefixation.

In a Tagalog corpus composed of books for elementary and high school students, the total token frequency of monomorphemic words starting with maN-/paN-/naN-phonological sequences is only 35.91 parts per million (ppm), while morphologically complex words with maN-, paN-, and naN-prefixes and the maprefix attached to nasal-initial stems have 8,369.88 ppm (see Supplementary Material B on OSF).
Plausibly, Tagalog listeners exploit the phonological sequences maN-/paN-/naN-as a cue to initiate decomposition, since they most often signify that the word is prefixed.

Further, these phonological sequences are followed by a consonant in nasal assimilation (e.g., mambúlag) and by a vowel in nasal substitution (e.g., mamangka) and in ma-prefixed words attached to nasal-initial stems (e.g., mamúlat).

Perhaps, hearing the next segment (i.e., a consonant or a vowel) after maN-/paN-/naN disambiguates between nasal assimilation vs. nasal substitution or ma-prefixation, potentially avoiding any misparsing.
The current data does not shed light as to how this disambiguation occurs.

This hypothesis should therefore be tested in future studies along similar lines to Gwilliams & Marantz (2015)'s study on Arabic, with a single word reading study with concurrent MEG recording, in which the evoked MEG signal is modelled as a function of morpheme vs. phoneme derived surprisal measures.
text.formatted: This hypothesis should therefore be tested in future studies along similar lines to Gwilliams & Marantz (2015)'s study on Arabic, with a single word reading study with concurrent MEG recording, in which the evoked MEG signal is modelled as a function of morpheme vs. phoneme derived surprisal measures.

text.text: This would allow a direct investigation of how parsing of prefixed words unfolds over time and uncover what cues listeners use to trigger decomposition.

Overall, the present findings indicate that auditory decomposition is equally rapid and easy for prefixed words without morphophonological alternation, with nasal assimilation, and with nasal substitution.
Previous models of morphological processing have not explicitly considered nasal assimilation and nasal substitution, but some may offer mechanistic accounts.

In underspecification-based accounts, phonological changes are accommodated by allowing the phonological representation of morphemes to be underspecified with respect to those aspects of the input that change in certain morphological contexts (Marslen-Wilson & Zhou, 1999; Reid & Marslen-Wilson, 2003).
text.formatted: In underspecification-based accounts, phonological changes are accommodated by allowing the phonological representation of morphemes to be underspecified with respect to those aspects of the input that change in certain morphological contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Marslen-Wilson & Zhou, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Reid & Marslen-Wilson, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: For example, the prefix /maŋ-/ and the stem /bangká/ 'boat' would be represented as [ma_]+[_angká] in the phonological lexicon, allowing for successful retrieval of each morpheme when they surface as full forms (e.g., maŋ-hula 'to guess', bangkáin 'use a boat') and as altered forms (e.g., mamangká 'to go boating'), since there will be no mismatch in the phonological representation and the segmented pieces at the surface level.

Alternatively, the readjustment-based account proposes that morphophonological operations are undone in the initial stage of processing while keeping the phonological representation of morphemes fully specified (Stockall & Gwilliams, forthcoming).
text.formatted: Alternatively, the readjustment-based account proposes that morphophonological operations are undone in the initial stage of processing while keeping the phonological representation of morphemes fully specified <ref type="bibr">(Stockall & Gwilliams, forthcoming)</ref>.

text.text: Based on this proposal, the nasal substitution operation in mamangká ([/maŋ-/➔ [mam-]/_ [p, b]) would first be undone during decomposition, which would then allow the retrieval of the vocabulary items /maŋ-/+/bangká/.
text.formatted: Based on this proposal, the nasal substitution operation in mamangká ([/maŋ-/➔ [mam-]/_ <ref type="bibr">[p, b]</ref>) would first be undone during decomposition, which would then allow the retrieval of the vocabulary items /maŋ-/+/bangká/.

text.text: Perhaps, future auditory experiments can quantify the reliability of different morphophonological rules and examine how they affect decomposition, in order to tease apart which account is more plausible with respect to words that undergo morphophonological alternations.

To conclude, our results provide further evidence supporting the validity of the auditory masked priming paradigm in investigating morphological decomposition processes in speech comprehension (Kouider & Dupoux, 2005; Ussishkin et al., 2015 Ussishkin et al., , 2017 Ussishkin et al., , 2025;; Pizarro-Guevara, 2017).
text.formatted: To conclude, our results provide further evidence supporting the validity of the auditory masked priming paradigm in investigating morphological decomposition processes in speech comprehension <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Kouider & Dupoux, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Ussishkin et al., 2015</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Ussishkin et al., , 2017</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Ussishkin et al., , 2025;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Pizarro-Guevara, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Building on earlier findings from auditory masked priming studies, we show that listeners successfully recognise morphemes within prefixed words despite morphophonological alternations that obscure the phonological identities of prefix and stem, as well as their morphological boundary.

Further, listeners also successfully link the obscured form of the stem like in mamangká to their unchanged stem form like bangká, suggesting that these stems are linked together in the mental lexicon in such a way that speakers and listeners represent them as forms of the same stem.

We also show that decomposition in speech comprehension occurs even when the listener has to deal with morphophonological variability that may cause uncertainty on where the morphological boundary is (e.g., /maŋ-/+/bangká/ becomes ma-mangka 'to go boating' vs. /maŋ-/+/búlag/ becomes mam-búlag 'to blind').

Taken together, these findings extend our theoretical understanding of how robust decomposition of a word into its constituent morphemes is in speech comprehension, and this contribution is only made possible by looking at an understudied language, Tagalog.

We call for future research to look at other understudied languages with unique morphophonological operations in order to establish a more comprehensive understanding of morphological processing in different modalities.

All data were collected [1] NOCHANGE, consisting of prefixed words with no morphophonological alternations (maŋ-, paŋ-prefixes attached to h-initial, y-initial, and nasal-initial sounds); [2] ASSIMILATION, consisting of nasal-assimilated prefixed words; and [3] SUBSTITUTION, consisting of nasal-substituted prefixed words.

Within the SUBSTITUTION condition, we created two sub-conditions with 20 trials each: VOICED condition, which consisted of nasal-substituted prefixed words with voiced-initial stems (the less common pattern), and VOICELESS condition, which consisted of nasal-substituted prefixed words with voiceless-initial stems (the more common pattern).
Across all conditions, the target words were each preceded by either a morphologically related prime or a morphologically unrelated prime (20 related, 20 unrelated).
The prefixes maŋ-and paŋ-were used in all key conditions.

Responses were recorded using the keyboard on participants' computers, which measured lexical decision response time (RT) as well as lexical decision accuracy.
In each trial, participants performed a lexical decision on the target in each prime-target stimulus pair by pressing the corresponding arrow key.
For half of the participants, 'Oo' (Yes) mapped to the left arrow key and 'Hindi' (No) mapped to the right arrow key, while the other half experienced the opposite mapping.
Button press counterbalancing was independent of block order.

Participants were instructed to respond as quickly and as accurately as possible to each target, with a time-out of 2000 ms; participants who failed to respond within 2000 ms of trial offset received a visual time-out message ('no response detected') and were then presented with the subsequent trial.

We set NOCHANGE and RELATED as reference levels for CONDITION and PRIMETYPE, respectively.

To further test whether phonological variability affects decomposition, we also ran further analyses on the two sub-conditions within SUBSTITUTION: VOICELESS, with voiceless-initial stems, and VOICED, with voiced-initial stems.The fixed effects were STEMC (VOICELESS, VOICED) and PRIMETYPE (RELATED, UNRELATED), as well as their interaction.

We found reliable priming effects in the IDENTITY condition while no such effects were found for the PHONCON condition, thereby supporting the validity of auditory masked priming in Tagalog and in a fully online setting.

Further, reliable priming effects of similar magnitude were also observed in the NOCHANGE, ASSIMILATION, and SUBSTITUTION conditions, suggesting that prefixed words were decomposed into morphemes during auditory word recognition, regardless of whether there is an obscurity in the prefix identity only (ASSIMILATION), or additional obscurity in the /prefix/+/stem/ boundary (SUBSTITUTION).

Results from this experiment are consistent with the findings ofCayado et al. (2025), where prefixed words were decomposed into morphemes during visual word recognition, regardless of nasal assimilation or nasal substitution that visually obscured the morpheme boundary.

Overall, the present findings and those ofCayado et al. (2025)  unambiguously show that decomposition in both visual and auditory domains remains robust and operational in the face of variable morphophonological alternations that obscure morphological identities and boundaries at the orthographic and phonological levels.
